paragraphs: In one school, an examiner was testing a group of young children, and rather unwisely he loaded them with very hard questions. One of them was: why doesn't the earth fall? He hoped to draw out something about gravity or some other complicated scientific idea.
Most of the children didn't even understand what he was asking, and their answers were all over the place. But one clever little girl answered with a question of her own: where would it fall to?
Swamiji loved her reply. The examiner's question, he said, made no sense to begin with. In the universe there is no real up or down; such ideas are only relative.

The same is true of the soul, he explained. Asking about its birth and death is equally meaningless. Who is coming and who is going? Where are you not already? Which heaven could you go to that you are not in already? The Self is everywhere, so there is nowhere for it to go and nowhere it is not.

For the perfect, Swamiji said, the whole childish dream of birth and death, of higher and lower worlds, disappears at once. For those who are nearly perfect, it fades after they pass through the higher realms up to Brahmaloka. Only for the ignorant does it go on.
learn: Sometimes the smartest move is to question the question. Before stressing over a problem, check whether it is built on a false assumption; a simple, honest question can cut through a lot of confusion.
